title: AI Emergency Powers
description: What the US government could legally do to an AI company in a crisis using laws already on the books, how courts and Congress check those powers, and how new AI halt powers are being designed.
caveat: Facts current as of October 22, 2026, from statutes, court opinions, CRS reports and 2026 reporting. Several key questions have never been decided by a court, so legal views are attributed. Not legal advice. Written by Claude, an Anthropic model; Anthropic is a party to two 2026 disputes covered here. AI fact-checked; no person has reviewed it.

units.title: Where the power comes from
units.desc: The map for the whole course: emergency power comes from statutes Congress wrote, and the President on his own stands on weaker ground. Then what declaring a national emergency does, and doesn't do.

items.p: In 1952, during the Korean War, President Truman ordered the government to seize and run most of the nation's steel mills to head off a strike. No statute authorized it. How did the Supreme Court rule?
o: It struck the seizure down: the power had to come from a statute or the Constitution, and neither covered it
It upheld the seizure as a valid use of the commander-in-chief power while US troops were fighting in Korea
It upheld the seizure for the length of the war but required the government to compensate the owners
It declined to rule, calling a wartime seizure a political question for Congress and the President to settle
ow: The Court rejected the commander-in-chief argument for taking over private industry at home to keep a labor dispute from stopping production.
Compensation comes up in other seizure cases; here the seizure itself was held unlawful.
The Court decided the case on the merits, 6 to 3.
keys: struck down (Youngstown, 6 to 3)
no statute authorized it
no constitutional power covered it
items.x: Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer: 'The President's power, if any, to issue the order must stem either from an act of Congress or from the Constitution itself.' Congress had even rejected an emergency seizure amendment when it passed the Taft-Hartley Act in 1947. Later fights over emergency power, including over AI labs, usually start from this case.

items.p: Justice Jackson's concurrence in the 1952 steel seizure case sorts presidential actions into three zones. Match each situation to how strong the President's power is.
pairs: Congress authorized it, expressly or by implication
Power at its maximum: his own plus all Congress can delegate
Congress has neither granted nor denied the power
A zone of twilight, where the outcome depends on events
The action goes against Congress's stated or implied will
Power at its lowest ebb
items.x: Jackson's concurrence, not the majority opinion, became the test courts use. In Dames & Moore v. Regan (1981) the Court recast the zones as a spectrum running from explicit congressional authorization to explicit prohibition. For any AI crisis order, the first question is where on that spectrum it sits.

items.p: Justice Jackson put Truman's steel seizure in his weakest zone, where presidential power is at its 'lowest ebb.' Why that zone?
o: Congress had set its own procedures for seizures, and this seizure ignored them
No statute mentioned steel mills, so the President was acting where Congress was silent
The Korean War was undeclared, so the President's war powers did not apply
The mill owners had received no compensation when their mills were taken
ow: Silence would put it in the middle 'twilight' zone. Jackson said Congress had spoken: it had 'covered it by three statutory policies inconsistent with this seizure.'
Jackson's reasoning turned on what Congress had done, not on whether war was formally declared.
Compensation is a separate takings question; it doesn't decide which zone an action falls in.
keys: Congress had legislated on seizure, with conditions this seizure ignored
so the action went against Congress's will
items.x: Congress had rejected an emergency seizure amendment to the Taft-Hartley Act in 1947, and its labor laws set out other procedures. The lesson for AI: an order that cuts against a choice Congress made is far weaker than one acting where Congress said nothing.

items.p: When lawyers assess whether the President could force an AI lab to stop in a crisis, why do they look for a statute before considering the President's own constitutional powers?
items.answer: Because of Youngstown: without a statute, the President relies on his own constitutional powers, which the Court refused to stretch to seizing or running private industry at home. With a statute behind him, his power is at its maximum, and the legal fight narrows to what the statute covers.
keys: Youngstown: inherent power didn't cover taking over domestic industry
statutory authorization puts presidential power at its maximum (Jackson)
the dispute becomes about the statute's scope
items.x: In 2026 most of the government's formal moves against Anthropic rested on existing statutes: export controls and procurement law, with the Defense Production Act threatened. The President's directive to stop using Anthropic's technology cited no law. The open questions were how far those statutes stretch.

choice.p: Why do lawyers assessing a crisis order against an AI lab look first for a statute rather than the President's own constitutional powers?
o: After Youngstown, inherent power is weak at home; a statute puts it at its maximum
The Constitution limits the President's emergency powers to crises abroad, leaving domestic problems to the states
Actions taken under a statute can't be challenged in court, while constitutional claims can be
Using constitutional powers requires Senate consent, while acting under a statute does not
ow: Youngstown didn't rule out all domestic emergency power; it held this seizure unauthorized.
Actions under statutes are challenged in court all the time, as the 2026 Anthropic cases show.
No Senate-consent rule applies to the President's use of his own powers.

items.p: Match each legal tool to the main leverage it gives the government over an AI company.
pairs: Export controls (ECRA, 2018)
Require a license before controlled technology reaches foreign parties, no emergency needed
IEEPA
Block dealings involving foreign interests, once a national emergency is declared
Defense Production Act
Make a company fill government orders first and hand over information
Procurement law
Stop buying from a company and exclude it as a supply-chain risk
items.x: These four tools get a unit each in this course. None was written to halt an AI lab, so the 2026 fights were about how far each one stretches. IEEPA is the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. A national emergency declaration adds no power of its own; it switches on statutes like IEEPA.

items.p: On its own, what does a national emergency declaration under the National Emergencies Act (1976) give the President?
o: Only the emergency powers found in other statutes, which he must name
A general power to take whatever steps the emergency requires
Authority to suspend court review of actions taken during the emergency
Authority to set aside any federal statute that gets in the way of the response
ow: The Act is procedural: it lets the President declare an emergency 'with respect to' Acts of Congress that grant emergency powers.
Courts still review actions taken under emergency statutes, and the Act gives no power to suspend that review.
A declaration activates other statutes; it can't override them.
keys: activates only powers in other statutes that are conditioned on an emergency
the President must specify which provisions he will use
items.x: 50 U.S.C. 1631 bars using emergency powers 'unless and until the President specifies the provisions of law under which he proposes that he, or other officers will act.' The Brennan Center counts 137 statutory powers that a declaration can make available.

items.p: How long do national emergencies under the National Emergencies Act tend to last in practice?
o: Often for decades, because the President can renew each one with a routine yearly notice
About a year, since each one ends a year after it is declared unless Congress extends it
About six months, since Congress must vote every six months to keep each one in force
Until the next emergency is declared, since a new declaration replaces the one before it
ow: An emergency lapses at its anniversary only if the President doesn't renew it, and renewal is a routine Federal Register notice.
The law says each House 'shall meet' every six months to consider a vote, but CRS reports neither chamber has ever done so for an IEEPA emergency.
Each threat gets its own declaration, and dozens run side by side (51 as of October 2026, per the Brennan Center).
keys: often years or decades
renewal is a routine yearly notice by the President
Congress has never used the six-month review to end an IEEPA emergency
items.x: The Brennan Center counted 51 declared emergencies in effect as of October 19, 2026. Carter's November 1979 emergency over Iran, the first under IEEPA, is still running. An emergency declared in an AI crisis could easily outlast the crisis.

items.p: In 2019, for the first time, both chambers of Congress passed a resolution to end a national emergency: President Trump's emergency at the southern border, used to fund wall construction. What happened next?
o: Trump vetoed it, and the House fell short of the two-thirds needed to override
The emergency ended at once, since both chambers had voted by majority to terminate it
The Supreme Court struck the resolution down under INS v. Chadha
Senate leaders kept it from reaching the President by never formally sending the passed resolution to him
ow: A joint resolution needs the President's signature or a veto override to take effect.
Chadha struck down resolutions that bypass the President; this one went to him, as the 1985 fix requires.
It was sent to the President, who vetoed it.
keys: Trump vetoed it
the House couldn't reach the two-thirds needed to override
items.x: The Senate passed H.J.Res. 46 by 59 to 41; Trump vetoed it on March 15, 2019, and the House override failed 248 to 181. Majorities in both chambers weren't enough, which is why some reform bills would make emergencies lapse unless Congress votes to approve them.

items.p: The 1976 National Emergencies Act gave Congress an easy way to end emergencies. Why is that check much weaker today?
items.answer: The original Act let Congress end an emergency by concurrent resolution, with no presidential signature. After the Supreme Court struck down that kind of legislative veto in INS v. Chadha (1983), Congress switched in 1985 to a joint resolution, which the President can veto, so ending an emergency over his objection takes two-thirds of both chambers.
keys: originally a concurrent resolution, no signature needed
INS v. Chadha (1983) struck down legislative vetoes
now a joint resolution the President can veto, so two-thirds needed
items.x: CRS describes the 1985 change as 'significantly increasing the difficulty of terminating an emergency.' Reformers draw a design lesson for AI halt powers: a check that works only when Congress can override a veto is a weak one.

choice.p: Why is Congress's power to end national emergencies weaker than the 1976 law intended?
o: A 1983 ruling against legislative vetoes forced a switch to a joint resolution the President can veto
Congress handed its power to end emergencies to the federal courts in a 1985 amendment to the Act
The steel seizure case gave the President the final say over when a declared emergency ends
A 2001 law made resolutions ending an emergency need 60 votes in the Senate, like most bills
ow: Courts gained no such power; the 1985 change was from a concurrent to a joint resolution.
The steel seizure case (1952) came long before the Act and dealt with a seizure, not ending emergencies.
No such law exists; the Senate passed a termination resolution 59 to 41 in 2019 under the Act's fast-track rules.

units.title: IEEPA: power over foreign dealings
units.desc: The International Emergency Economic Powers Act is the sanctions law. It's powerful against threats from abroad, has built-in exceptions, and fits a purely American company badly.

items.p: IEEPA (the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, 1977) is the main US sanctions law. What has to be true before a President can use it?
o: He has declared a national emergency over an unusual and extraordinary threat from abroad
Congress has approved the emergency by joint resolution within 30 days of its declaration
The United States is engaged in armed hostilities with the country whose assets are targeted
The Secretary of State has certified the target country as a sponsor of terrorism
ow: No approval from Congress is needed; IEEPA powers are available as soon as the President declares the emergency.
Hostilities matter only for IEEPA's narrower power to confiscate property.
That certification triggers other laws; IEEPA needs only a declared emergency over a threat from abroad.
keys: national emergency declaration
unusual and extraordinary threat
source in whole or substantial part outside the US
items.x: 50 U.S.C. 1701: the threat must have 'its source in whole or substantial part outside the United States' and endanger national security, foreign policy or the economy. Each new threat needs its own declaration. As of September 2025, CRS counted 77 IEEPA emergencies declared, 46 still ongoing.

items.p: Once an IEEPA emergency is declared, what can the President do?
o: Block or prohibit transactions involving property that a foreign country or national has an interest in
Seize and keep foreign-owned property in the United States in peacetime, without paying for it
Set the prices that US companies may charge for goods and services connected to the threat
Take temporary control of US companies whose products or services are tied to the threat, until it passes
ow: IEEPA allows confiscation only when the US is in armed hostilities or has been attacked. That limited power was added in 2001; the 1977 law allowed no confiscation at all.
IEEPA regulates transactions involving foreign interests and gives no price-setting power; the DPA's price controls need a joint resolution of Congress.
IEEPA regulates transactions; it gives no power to take over companies.
keys: block, regulate or prohibit transactions
property in which a foreign country or national has any interest
items.x: 50 U.S.C. 1702 lets the President 'investigate, block during the pendency of an investigation, regulate, direct and compel, nullify, void, prevent or prohibit' such transactions. Freezing assets and barring dealings with named foreign companies are the classic uses. The power runs through foreign interests, which is why its reach over a purely domestic company is doubtful.

items.p: A colleague says Commerce must have declared a national emergency to restrict exports of an AI model, 'since export controls are IEEPA powers.' What's the correction?
o: Since 2018, export controls rest on a standing law (ECRA); IEEPA only filled in while an older law had lapsed
Export controls do need an emergency, but the Commerce Secretary declares it, not the President
Export controls come from the President's own foreign affairs power under Article II, so they need no statute
Export controls are IEEPA powers, but emergencies covering technology never expire
ow: No emergency declaration is needed under ECRA, by anyone.
Congress passed ECRA in 2018 to give the export rules a firm statutory basis.
ECRA replaced the IEEPA stopgap; the rules no longer depend on an emergency.
keys: export controls rest on the Export Control Reform Act (2018)
a standing statute, no emergency needed
IEEPA was a stopgap while the Export Administration Act had lapsed
items.x: When the old Export Administration Act lapsed, Presidents kept the export rules running with IEEPA emergencies, most recently one declared in 2001. The Export Control Reform Act of 2018 gave the rules a standing basis. The 2001 emergency is still renewed each year for a few leftover sanctions provisions, but the core export rules no longer depend on it, and Congress can't switch them off by ending an emergency.

items.p: Why would it be legally difficult to use IEEPA to order a purely American AI lab, with no foreign ties, to stop serving US customers?
items.answer: IEEPA can be used only against a threat whose source is wholly or substantially outside the US, and its powers reach transactions in property in which a foreign country or national has an interest. The 1977 Senate committee report said power over purely domestic transactions would not be granted. A lab with no foreign link fits neither hook.
keys: the threat must come largely from outside the US
powers reach only property with a foreign interest
Congress's committee report excluded purely domestic transactions
items.x: The limit may be thinner than it looks: a scholar cited by CRS called the domestic exemption 'a limitation without substance,' since few big companies lack any foreign investor, customer or employee. Real labs have many foreign ties.

choice.p: Why would IEEPA be hard to use against a purely American AI lab with no foreign ties?
o: It needs a threat from abroad and reaches only property with a foreign interest
It can be used only after Congress approves the emergency by joint resolution within 30 days
It covers only physical goods, so software and AI models are excluded
Its powers lapse in December 2026 unless Congress renews them, like the Defense Production Act's
ow: No congressional approval is required; that's a reform proposal, and it would exempt IEEPA anyway.
IEEPA reaches transactions of all kinds, not only goods.
IEEPA has no sunset; the Defense Production Act's core powers are the ones that expire.

items.p: In 2020, President Trump used IEEPA to bar transactions with TikTok. TikTok and groups of its users sued. What did the courts do?
o: Blocked them, mainly because IEEPA exempts informational materials and personal communications
Upheld the measures, deferring to the President's judgment about national security threats under IEEPA
Blocked the measures because the President hadn't asked Congress to approve the emergency
Dismissed the suits because IEEPA bars courts from reviewing actions taken under it
ow: Three courts blocked the measures, and the government's appeals were dismissed in 2021.
IEEPA needs no approval from Congress.
IEEPA lets the government show classified evidence privately but doesn't bar review; these courts reviewed and blocked the measures.
keys: courts blocked the measures
IEEPA's exceptions for informational materials and personal communications
items.x: One court found TikTok videos 'analogous to the films, artworks, photographs, and news wire feeds' IEEPA protects; another said the bans likely regulated personal communications or information indirectly. The WeChat court relied on the First Amendment. In 2024 Congress passed a separate law requiring TikTok's divestiture.

items.p: IEEPA bars the President from regulating 'informational materials,' in any format, even indirectly. Why could that exception matter if IEEPA were used against an AI model?
items.answer: A lab could argue that its model's outputs are informational materials, which IEEPA can't regulate directly or indirectly. Whether they count is an open question, so an IEEPA order aimed at a model would invite that challenge.
keys: a lab could argue model outputs are protected informational materials
the exception applies regardless of format and bars indirect regulation
whether AI outputs count is unsettled
items.x: 50 U.S.C. 1702(b) (the Berman Amendment of 1988, widened in 1994) applies 'regardless of format or medium of transmission.' IEEPA also exempts personal communications, humanitarian donations and travel. The TikTok rulings read these exceptions broadly; as of October 2026, whether AI outputs count was an open question.

choice.p: Why could IEEPA's exception for 'informational materials' matter if IEEPA were used against an AI model?
o: A lab could argue the model's outputs are informational materials, an unsettled question
It limits IEEPA to physical goods, which would leave software products like AI models outside the law
It protects companies that publish their safety research, which most frontier AI labs do
It requires a court order before the President can regulate a service that transmits information
ow: IEEPA reaches transactions in services and software too; the exception covers informational materials specifically.
The exception protects the materials themselves; publishing research doesn't exempt a company.
IEEPA needs no court order; the exception removes informational materials from its reach altogether.

items.p: In 2025 the President imposed sweeping tariffs under IEEPA emergencies. In February 2026 the Supreme Court decided the challenge (Learning Resources v. Trump). What did it hold?
o: IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, 6 to 3, because the power to 'regulate' doesn't include the power to tax
IEEPA is unconstitutional, 6 to 3, because it hands Congress's power over trade to the President without limits
The tariffs were valid because the emergencies had been properly declared and renewed
Trade emergencies are political questions, so the Court left the tariffs in place
ow: The Court read the statute narrowly. It didn't strike IEEPA down, and IEEPA's sanctions powers are untouched.
The Court didn't rule on the declarations. It held that IEEPA doesn't authorize tariffs, even with an emergency declared.
The Court decided the merits and held that IEEPA gives the President no power to impose tariffs.
keys: IEEPA does not authorize tariffs
6 to 3, based on the statute's text: regulating is not taxing
items.x: Chief Justice Roberts, for six justices, said the Court was skeptical that Congress had hidden its power to tax inside IEEPA's ordinary power to 'regulate.' Lesson for AI: a declared emergency doesn't stretch a statute beyond its text.

items.p: A lawyer argues an old emergency statute could support halting frontier AI, because courts read emergency powers broadly in a crisis. What does the 2026 tariff case suggest in reply?
o: Emergency laws are read by their text, and three justices said major new uses need clear authorization
Emergency statutes are now off limits, because the Court struck IEEPA down as unconstitutional
Courts defer on national security in emergencies, so the lawyer's argument would likely succeed
The case moved the power to declare emergencies to Congress, so a President's halt order would be void
ow: The Court read IEEPA narrowly and didn't strike it down; its sanctions powers are untouched.
The Court ruled against the President on the merits despite the declared emergencies.
Declarations stay with the President; the case limited what IEEPA itself allows.
keys: a declared emergency doesn't stretch a statute beyond its text
three justices: the major questions doctrine applies to emergency statutes too
clear authorization from Congress needed for major new uses
items.x: The major questions doctrine says that for decisions of vast economic or political significance, the government must point to clear authorization from Congress. Only Roberts, Gorsuch and Barrett joined this part; three other justices agreed the tariffs were unlawful on the text alone. Halting frontier AI under a 1977 law would invite exactly this argument.

units.title: Export controls: the switch already used
units.desc: Export controls run on a standing law, move fast, and reach people inside the US. In June 2026 a Commerce directive led Anthropic to take two frontier models offline worldwide.

news.h: Two new Anthropic models go offline for all users after a Commerce export-control directive

items.p: Why did Commerce's June 2026 directive on Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models lead to a worldwide shutdown?
o: It barred foreign nationals, including Anthropic's staff; unable to check nationality, Anthropic shut both off
It ordered Anthropic to shut both models down worldwide until government testers had finished evaluating them
It barred access from China and Russia, and Anthropic shut the models down globally in protest
Anthropic paused the models on its own after a jailbreak report, and the directive formalized that pause
ow: The directive covered foreign nationals; the global shutoff was Anthropic's way of complying.
It covered foreign nationals generally, not particular countries.
Anthropic suspended the models in response to the directive.
keys: barred access by foreign nationals, including Anthropic's own employees
Anthropic couldn't verify nationality in real time
so it suspended both models for all users
items.x: The restriction was lifted June 30 after Anthropic agreed to commitments including pre-release government testing and sharing jailbreak findings. Both sides trace the order to a partner company's report of a way around Fable 5's safeguards; Anthropic says Amazon researchers wrote it. They disagree on how serious it was: the government's account, relayed by David Sacks (by then co-chair of the President's science and technology council, PCAST), called it a path to a cyber weapon and said Anthropic refused to fix the flaw or pull the model; Anthropic called it a narrow jailbreak exposing capabilities other models already had.

items.p: Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) can impose a new export restriction overnight, without the public notice-and-comment process most agency rules need. Why?
o: ECRA exempts its actions from the Administrative Procedure Act's rulemaking and court review rules
Each restriction counts as a national emergency, which suspends the normal agency procedures
The President personally signs each restriction, and presidential orders skip notice and comment
Congress approves the year's restrictions in advance in the annual defense authorization bill
ow: The export control law (ECRA) needs no emergency declaration.
BIS acts on its own authority under ECRA; the President doesn't sign each restriction.
Congress doesn't vote on individual export restrictions.
keys: ECRA exempts export-control functions from the Administrative Procedure Act
no notice-and-comment requirement or APA court review
items.x: 50 U.S.C. 4821 says ECRA functions 'shall not be subject to' the Administrative Procedure Act's rulemaking and judicial review sections. That speed helps in a crisis. It also meant the June 2026 restriction on two AI models took effect with no public comment, and critics said it came with no public criteria.

items.p: A US lab gives a foreign-national engineer in its California office access to export-controlled technology. Under US export rules, what is that?
o: A 'deemed export' to the engineer's home country, which may need a license
Not an export, since the technology stays inside the United States
An export once the engineer later carries the technology out of the country
An immigration matter for the State Department, outside the export rules
ow: Releasing controlled technology to a foreign person inside the US is treated as an export.
The release itself counts, wherever the person goes afterward.
Commerce's export rules govern this, not immigration law.
keys: deemed export
treated as an export to the person's most recent country of citizenship or permanent residency
items.x: 15 C.F.R. 734.13: 'Any release in the United States of technology or source code to a foreign person is a deemed export to the foreign person's most recent country of citizenship or permanent residency.' This rule explains why the June 2026 restriction on two AI models reached Anthropic's own staff.

items.p: Why are open-weight AI models (whose weights anyone can download) hard to restrict with export controls?
o: Unclassified technology made public with no limits on sharing counts as 'published' and is outside the rules
Open-source licenses are legally binding contracts that override federal export regulations
Commerce's export authority covers physical goods such as chips, leaving software and model weights outside it
Open-weight models are trained below the compute thresholds that trigger US export controls on weights
ow: Licenses are private agreements; they can't override federal law.
The export rules cover software and technology as well as goods.
Some open-weight models are very large; the exclusion turns on publication, not size.
keys: published information is not subject to the export rules (EAR)
made available to the public without restrictions on further dissemination
items.x: 15 C.F.R. 734.7 puts 'published' technology and software outside the rules. The 2025 AI Diffusion rule said: 'BIS is not imposing controls on the model weights of open-weight models.' Once weights are public, there's nothing left to license.

items.p: Match each export-control tool to what it does.
pairs: Entity List
Names foreign parties that need a license to receive covered items
Foreign direct product rule
Reaches foreign-made items produced with US technology or tools
'Is informed' letter
BIS tells a specific party that a license is now required
Deemed export
Release of controlled technology to a foreign person inside the US
items.x: The US used the Entity List and then an expanded foreign direct product rule against Huawei in 2019 and 2020, aiming export controls at a single company. PIIE's Martin Chorzempa describes the June 2026 directive on two Anthropic models as an 'is informed' letter applying deemed-export logic.

items.p: The January 2025 AI Diffusion rule was the first US export control on AI model weights. Which weights did it cover?
o: Closed-weight models trained with more than 10^26 operations; open-weight models were excluded
Models trained with more than 10^26 operations, whether their weights were open or closed
Models sold or licensed to customers based in China, whatever their training compute
The chips used to train frontier models; the model weights themselves stayed uncontrolled
ow: It expressly excluded open-weight models, since published weights fall outside the export rules.
It used a compute threshold and covered exports to most countries.
It created a new control on model weights themselves, alongside its chip rules.
keys: closed-weight models
trained with more than 10^26 operations
open-weight models excluded
items.x: The rule also exempted labs' regular employees from deemed-export limits, which matters for the June 2026 episode. BIS said in May 2025 it would rescind the rule and stopped enforcing it; as of its May 31, 2026 guidance it still wasn't enforcing it, and it had published no formal repeal.

items.p: Commerce's June 2026 directive on two Anthropic models reached the company's foreign-national staff working in the US. The 2025 AI Diffusion rule would not have. What difference explains this?
items.answer: Both treat sharing controlled technology with a foreign person in the US as an export (a deemed export). The 2025 Diffusion rule exempted labs' regular employees from that; the June 2026 directive had no carve-out for staff.
keys: deemed export: access by a foreign person in the US counts as an export
the Diffusion rule exempted labs' regular employees
the June directive had no staff carve-out
items.x: PIIE's Martin Chorzempa describes the order as treating a non-citizen Anthropic engineer's access like an export to that engineer's country. The directive's text and legal basis were not made public at the time, so its exact legal form is inferred from reporting and from the export-license wording of the letter that lifted it.

choice.p: Why did the June 2026 directive reach Anthropic's US-based foreign-national staff when the 2025 Diffusion rule would not have?
o: The 2025 rule exempted labs' regular employees from deemed-export limits; the directive didn't
The directive was issued under IEEPA, which reaches property in which a foreign national has an interest
The 2025 rule covered open-weight models, which the staff could already download anyway
The directive relied on a new 2026 law that extended export rules to company employees
ow: Reporting describes an export-control directive from Commerce, and no IEEPA emergency was cited.
The 2025 rule covered closed-weight models; open-weight models were excluded.
No new law was involved; the directive applied existing deemed-export logic.

items.p: Legal analysts say the June 2026 episode raised a question about export controls that no court has settled. What is it?
o: Whether letting people use a model online counts as an 'export' Commerce can control
Whether Commerce can restrict exports of the most advanced AI chips to buyers based in China
Whether Commerce can put a US company on the Entity List to restrict its sales abroad
Whether the EU AI Act limits US export controls on models that are sold to customers in Europe
ow: Chip controls have been in place since 2022 and weren't the open question here.
The Entity List names foreign parties; the June directive was a letter to a US company about who could use its models.
EU law doesn't govern US export controls.
keys: whether remote or API access to a model counts as an export
export rules traditionally cover transfers of goods and technology, not access to services
items.x: Lawfare's Alan Rozenshtein (who also works at Anthropic) calls the question unsettled, and PIIE's Martin Chorzempa notes export jurisdiction doesn't usually cover access to services. The House passed the Remote Access Security Act 369 to 22 in January 2026 to address remote access, but the Senate hadn't acted as of October 2026.

items.p: Critics argued that restricting a top US model the way Commerce did in June 2026 could end up helping China. What mechanism did they point to?
o: Foreign buyers fearing a US off switch would move to Chinese open-weight models, which have none
Chinese labs could copy the model by training on its outputs through foreign resellers
The shutdown handed Chinese labs months of scarce chip capacity that would otherwise have gone to Anthropic
Pausing a top US model would leave Chinese models ahead on public benchmarks for months
ow: Restricting access makes copying a model through its outputs harder; the critics' worry was buyers' trust.
A temporary access restriction doesn't transfer chips or compute to other labs.
The restriction lasted under three weeks; the critics' concern was long-run trust in US models that can be switched off.
keys: foreign buyers lose trust in US models that can be switched off
they shift to Chinese open-weight models that can't be
items.x: PIIE's Martin Chorzempa (who disclosed joining two amicus briefs on Anthropic's side) made this argument, noting the order had no carve-outs even for close allies, and relays French President Macron's warning that France would not buy US AI models that can simply be switched off. Pentagon CIO Kirsten Davies backed the move as putting national security ahead of revenue.

items.p: Name two process problems critics identified in how the government restricted two Anthropic models in June 2026.
items.answer: Examples: no public criteria for when a model gets restricted; the legal basis and the order itself were not published; no carve-outs for close allies; no set procedure for a company to get access restored; no insulation from impulse or political favoritism.
keys: no public criteria
legal basis never published
no carve-outs for allies
no procedure to restore access
no protection against impulse or favoritism
items.x: Lawfare writers Klaassen and Frazier note there was no set procedure for restoring access. ARI's Brad Carson said such decisions need insulation from impulse and political favoritism. These gaps are what the AI-specific halt bills in a later unit try to fill.

choice.p: Which of these is a process problem critics identified in the June 2026 restriction on two Anthropic models?
o: There was no published legal basis and no set procedure for restoring access
It was issued under the Defense Production Act, which lets officials skip written findings
It covered users in China and Russia but left other risky foreign users unaffected
It was enforced through a court order that Anthropic had no chance to oppose
ow: It was a Commerce export-control directive; the Defense Production Act was threatened in a separate dispute.
It covered foreign nationals everywhere, including Anthropic's own staff; critics objected that even allies got no carve-out.
No court was involved; Commerce acted on its own export-control authority.

units.title: The Defense Production Act
units.desc: A 1950 law that lets the government put its orders first, fund production, compel information and bless industry agreements. It was threatened against an AI lab in 2026 but never used.

items.p: In March 2020, President Trump used the Defense Production Act on General Motors. What did the order do?
o: Required GM to accept, perform and prioritize federal contracts for ventilators
Put the federal government in charge of GM's factories for the length of the pandemic emergency
Set the price at which GM had to sell its ventilators to hospitals and state governments
Required GM to make ventilators at cost, with any profit on federal orders going back to the Treasury
ow: The DPA no longer allows requisition; the order worked through contracts.
The DPA can't impose price controls without a joint resolution of Congress.
The order dealt with accepting and prioritizing contracts, not profits.
keys: accept, perform and prioritize
federal contracts for ventilators
items.x: The memorandum directed HHS to 'require General Motors Company to accept, perform, and prioritize contracts or orders' for ventilators. Such 'rated orders' (rated DO or the higher DX) must be filled ahead of other customers' unrated orders. Applied to AI, the same tool could make a lab put government work first. It doesn't obviously let the government take over a company or stop it selling to the public.

items.p: Match each Defense Production Act authority to what it does.
pairs: Title I
Makes firms accept and prioritize government orders; allocates materials
Title III
Loans and purchase commitments to expand domestic production
Section 705
Compels reports, records, inspections and testimony
Section 708
Voluntary industry agreements with a defense against antitrust suits
items.x: The DPA was passed in 1950 for the Korean War. Its powers to requisition property and control prices lapsed in 1953. Section 708 is permanent. Titles I and III and most of Title VII expire on December 11, 2026 unless Congress renews them, though Section 705's information powers run for two more years after the law lapses.

items.p: A staffer proposes using the Defense Production Act to take over an AI lab's data center in a crisis, 'like Truman did with the steel mills.' What's wrong with the analogy?
o: Its power to take over property lapsed in 1953, and Truman's seizure didn't rely on the DPA
The DPA needs a declared war to operate, and the United States is not at war with anyone today
The DPA covers factories and manufacturing, so data centers and software fall outside it
The DPA allows a government takeover, but the company has to give its written consent first
ow: The DPA is used in peacetime, as with ventilators in 2020 and infant formula in 2022.
Title I covers 'services' as well as materials and facilities; the limit is on takeovers, not sectors.
The DPA can compel firms to accept contracts without consent; it just doesn't allow takeovers.
keys: the DPA's requisition authority lapsed in 1953 (repealed in 2009)
Truman relied on claimed inherent power, not the DPA
items.x: Title II (requisition) and the titles on prices, wages and credit lapsed in 1953 and were formally repealed in 2009. Truman claimed inherent power, and the Court rejected it. Any takeover today would need another statute and would trigger the Fifth Amendment's duty to pay just compensation.

items.p: A crisis plan would use the Defense Production Act's allocation power to steer AI chips away from civilian buyers. What does the law require before Title I can control distribution in the civilian market?
o: A finding that the material is scarce and critical, and defense needs can't otherwise be met
A national emergency declared under the National Emergencies Act that specifically covers the AI chip supply
Approval from Congress by joint resolution within 30 days of the allocation order
A finding by the Secretary of State that a foreign adversary controls the chip supply
ow: The DPA's allocation powers don't depend on an emergency declaration.
A joint resolution is required for wage and price controls, not allocations.
No such State Department finding appears in the DPA.
keys: the material is scarce and critical
defense needs can't otherwise be met without significant dislocation
items.x: 50 U.S.C. 4511(b) bars using Title I to 'control the general distribution of any material in the civilian market' without these findings. The limit suggests the DPA is better suited to putting government orders first than to restricting what companies sell to the public.

items.p: President Biden's 2023 AI executive order required developers to report on training runs above 10^26 operations. Which law did it use for that requirement?
o: The Defense Production Act's power to collect information
IEEPA, through a national emergency declared over AI risks
The Export Control Reform Act's licensing system
The National Emergencies Act on its own
ow: IEEPA powered a different part of the order: reports by cloud providers about foreign customers.
Export controls regulate transfers abroad, not domestic reporting.
The National Emergencies Act only switches on other emergency statutes.
keys: Defense Production Act
Section 705 information collection
items.x: Executive Order 14110 cited the DPA, and Commerce's 2024 proposed rule relied on Section 705, which lets the government compel reports and records 'by regulation, subpoena, or otherwise.' President Trump revoked the order on January 20, 2025. Section 705 is still law, so a future administration could use it again.

items.p: Why might AI labs that want to agree on slowing down together seek approval under Section 708 of the Defense Production Act?
items.answer: Section 708 lets the President approve voluntary agreements among companies to meet a threat to national defense, and participants get a legal defense against antitrust suits for qualifying conduct. A coordinated slowdown among competitors could otherwise look like an illegal agreement to restrict output.
keys: the President can approve voluntary industry agreements
participants get a defense against antitrust suits
a coordinated slowdown could otherwise look like an illegal output restraint
items.x: In September 2026, days after Anthropic's CEO called for pacing the frontier, a proposed class action (Buist v. Anthropic) accused several labs of an illegal restraint on output. Section 708 is permanent, but whether a slowdown would qualify as helping 'provide for the national defense' is untested. The CATS Act, a 2026 bill, would add a narrower AI-specific antitrust exemption.

choice.p: Why might AI labs that agree together to slow development want the protection of Section 708 of the Defense Production Act?
o: Rivals agreeing to slow down could face antitrust suits for illegally restricting output
Slowing development would break the labs' existing contracts with the Defense Department
Labs need DPA approval to change training schedules for models above a compute threshold
Without it, export rules would bar the labs from sharing safety findings with each other
ow: The concern is antitrust law, not breach of defense contracts.
No law requires DPA approval for changing training schedules.
The legal risk in coordinating is antitrust, not export controls.

items.p: As of October 2026, what is the status of the Defense Production Act's core powers (Title I priorities, Title III funding and most of Title VII)?
o: They expire on December 11, 2026 unless Congress extends them again
They are permanent, as they have been since the law passed in 1950
They lapsed at the end of 2025 and Congress decided not to renew them
The President renews them each year by notice, as with national emergencies
ow: Most DPA powers have always carried sunset dates that Congress renews.
Congress renewed them in December 2025 and again in September 2026.
Renewal takes an act of Congress, not a presidential notice.
keys: expire December 11, 2026
unless Congress extends them
items.x: The FY2026 defense bill moved the deadline from September 30, 2025 to September 30, 2026, and a September 2026 stopgap spending law moved it to December 11, 2026. Section 708 (voluntary agreements), Section 721 (CFIUS foreign investment review) and a few others are permanent.

units.title: Procurement as leverage
units.desc: Procurement law gives no power to order a lab to stop, but the government can stop buying from it. The 2026 Pentagon-Anthropic fight shows how far that goes.

items.p: What was the 2026 dispute between the Pentagon and Anthropic about?
o: The Pentagon wanted 'any lawful use' terms; Anthropic refused mass domestic surveillance and fully autonomous weapons
Anthropic wanted to end all of its military contracts after a wave of employee protests over its weapons work
The Pentagon accused Anthropic of selling models to customers in China in breach of export rules
Anthropic sued the Pentagon over unpaid invoices for work it had done under a classified intelligence contract
ow: Anthropic offered to support lawful national security uses, with two exceptions.
The export-control episode was a separate Commerce action in June.
The dispute was about limits on use, not payment.
keys: the Pentagon demanded 'any lawful use' contract terms
Anthropic refused two uses: mass domestic surveillance and fully autonomous weapons
items.x: The Defense Secretary's January 2026 AI strategy memo told Defense Department AI contracts to adopt 'any lawful use' language. The Pentagon said it had no interest in illegal mass surveillance or weapons without human involvement, and objected to a vendor limiting lawful military use. After Anthropic refused, the Pentagon threatened the Defense Production Act, the President directed agencies to stop using Anthropic's technology, and the Pentagon designated Anthropic a supply-chain risk.

items.p: Why would it be harder to use the Defense Production Act to make an AI lab retrain its model without safeguards than to make it supply its existing model to the government?
items.answer: Title I's priority powers were built to make firms accept and fill government orders for products they already make. Compelling a new product, such as a model retrained without its safeguards, is untested under the DPA and would invite statutory, major-questions and First Amendment challenges.
keys: Title I compels accepting and prioritizing orders for existing products
compelling a new product is untested under the DPA
would invite major-questions and First Amendment challenges
items.x: Alan Rozenshtein's Lawfare analysis of the 2026 dispute (he also works at Anthropic) drew this line, while calling the relevant power largely untested. The DPA was never invoked; the Pentagon instead designated Anthropic a supply-chain risk.

choice.p: Why would the DPA more easily support a demand for a lab's existing model than a demand to retrain it without safeguards?
o: Title I covers orders for existing products; a new product is untested and raises speech issues
The DPA's power to compel orders lapsed in 1953, so only voluntary supply contracts remain
The lab's existing contract terms would override the DPA, since that agreement came first
The DPA covers physical goods, and retraining a model is a service outside its reach
ow: The 1953 lapse covered requisition, price controls and a few other titles; Title I's priority powers remain in force until December 11, 2026.
A rated order takes priority over other contracts; private terms don't override the statute.
Title I covers 'services' as well as materials and facilities.

items.p: In March 2026 the Pentagon designated Anthropic a supply-chain risk under two different statutes, and Anthropic challenged both in court. As of October 2026, how had the cases come out?
o: A California court set aside one designation, while the D.C. Circuit upheld the other, 2 to 1
Both designations were struck down as unlawful retaliation for Anthropic's public positions
Both designations were upheld, since courts traditionally defer to the military on what it chooses to buy
The cases ended in a settlement once Anthropic accepted the Pentagon's 'any lawful use' contract terms
ow: The D.C. Circuit found no First Amendment violation under the statute it reviewed.
Judge Rita Lin in California set aside the designation made under 10 U.S.C. 3252.
There was no settlement; in October 2026 Anthropic reportedly asked the full D.C. Circuit to rehear the case.
keys: a California federal court set aside the 10 U.S.C. 3252 designation (August 2026)
the D.C. Circuit upheld the FASCSA designation, 2 to 1 (September 2026)
items.x: Judge Rita Lin's August 27, 2026 ruling set aside the designation under 10 U.S.C. 3252 and permanently barred it, subject to appeal. On September 25 the D.C. Circuit (Judges Katsas and Rao, with Henderson dissenting) upheld the designation under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act (FASCSA), saying it had no quarrel with the California ruling because the statutes differ.

items.p: Two courts reached opposite results on the Pentagon's 2026 supply-chain-risk designations of Anthropic without contradicting each other. What difference between the two statutes explains this?
items.answer: 10 U.S.C. 3252 defines supply-chain risk as the risk that an adversary may sabotage or subvert a system, and the California court held Anthropic's contract stance didn't fit. The procurement statute FASCSA covers the risk that any person may sabotage or manipulate covered products, so the D.C. Circuit said no adversary or bad motive was needed.
keys: 10 U.S.C. 3252 requires a risk from an adversary
FASCSA covers risk from any person
no adversary or bad motive needed under FASCSA
items.x: The D.C. Circuit majority reasoned that Anthropic could change Claude through training in ways that hinder military use. The law firm Willkie Farr called the use of Section 3252 against an American company apparently unprecedented, saying it had been used before against foreign firms such as Kaspersky and Huawei.

choice.p: Why could courts uphold one Pentagon supply-chain designation of Anthropic and set aside the other?
o: One statute requires a risk from an 'adversary'; the other covers risk from 'any person'
One court held that the First Amendment protects companies and the other held it doesn't
One designation came from the President and the other from the Defense Secretary
One designation was made before the DPA threat and the other after it, so different rules applied
ow: Companies do have First Amendment rights; the D.C. Circuit found no violation on its facts.
Both formal designations came from the Defense Department.
Timing relative to the DPA threat wasn't what decided the cases.

items.p: A supply-chain-risk designation can't order a lab to stop deploying a model. Why can being excluded from government purchasing still be strong leverage over an AI company?
items.answer: The government is a very large customer, and exclusion spreads: agencies drop the product, contractors may avoid it to protect their own government work, and the company loses revenue, partners and standing. That pressure can push a lab to accept terms with no statute authorizing a halt.
keys: the government is a huge buyer
exclusion spreads to other agencies and contractors
pressure without any legal power to halt
items.x: After the February 2026 directives, GSA removed Anthropic from its USAi.gov platform and its main purchasing schedule, which Venable described as carrying out the President's all-agency directive. The Defense Secretary also claimed no military contractor could do any commercial business with Anthropic, a claim Willkie Farr said appears to go beyond the statute.

choice.p: Why can excluding an AI company from federal purchasing be strong leverage even though it can't order a halt?
o: Exclusion costs revenue and can spread to contractors and partners who need government business
Excluded companies also lose their Commerce Department export licenses until the designation ends
Exclusion lets the government take possession of the company's model weights and source code
Excluded companies are barred by federal law from raising money from US investors until the designation ends
ow: Export licensing is a separate system run by Commerce.
Purchasing law gives the government no power to take property.
No law bars excluded companies from raising private capital.

units.title: Other levers on the shelf
units.desc: Communications powers, the 2026 voluntary review order, cyber directives and other standing tools: what each can and can't do to an AI lab.

lessons.title: What else is on the books

items.p: Section 706 of the Communications Act lets the President close or take over communications facilities in some situations. Why would it be hard to use against an AI lab's cloud services in peacetime?
o: Its wire power needs a proclaimed state or threat of war, and its reach to AI services is unclear
It needs Congress to approve each takeover by joint resolution within 48 hours of the order
It was repealed when Congress rewrote the Communications Act in the Telecommunications Act of 1996
It requires the FCC to find that a network is being used to carry out an attack on the US
ow: Section 706 requires no approval from Congress.
Section 706 is still law, at 47 U.S.C. 606.
Section 706 gives the FCC no trigger role; the President acts on a proclamation or, for radio, a broader emergency finding.
keys: wire facilities: needs a proclamation of a state or threat of war
the broader national-emergency trigger covers only radio
its reach to cloud or AI services is unclear
items.x: 47 U.S.C. 606(d) covers wire facilities only on proclamation of 'a state or threat of war involving the United States,' while 606(c) covers radio in 'war or a threat of war, or a state of public peril or disaster or other national emergency.' Either way, owners get just compensation when the government takes over their facilities. Whether it could reach cloud or AI services is an open question.

items.p: What does the June 2026 executive order on frontier AI security (EO 14409) require of AI developers?
o: Nothing mandatory: agencies were told to design a voluntary framework for early government access
A 30-day government review that every frontier model must pass before it can be released to the public
A Commerce Department license for any model above a capability threshold set by the NSA
Reports on every training run above 10^26 operations under the Defense Production Act
ow: The framework is voluntary; the order says it doesn't authorize 'a mandatory governmental licensing, preclearance, or permitting requirement.'
The order says nothing in its framework section authorizes a mandatory licensing or preclearance requirement.
The order invokes no Defense Production Act authority.
keys: a voluntary framework
government access up to 30 days before release to other trusted partners
expressly no mandatory licensing or preclearance
items.x: The NSA Director decides which models are 'covered' through a classified cyber benchmarking process. The order cites only 'the Constitution and the laws of the United States' and names no emergency statute. Because it is voluntary, the government's hard leverage over labs in 2026 came from other tools.

items.p: Could CISA, the federal cybersecurity agency, use a Binding Operational Directive to order an AI lab to shut down a dangerous model?
o: No: these directives bind federal agencies' own information systems, not private companies
Yes: they bind operators of critical infrastructure, and frontier AI labs count as critical infrastructure
Yes, once the President has declared a national emergency covering the dangerous model
No: binding cybersecurity orders to private companies come from the FCC instead
ow: The law defines them as 'a compulsory direction to an agency,' not to private firms.
An emergency declaration doesn't extend these directives to private companies.
The FCC has no general power to order AI labs to shut down models.
keys: Binding Operational Directives bind federal agencies only
they don't reach private companies
items.x: 44 U.S.C. 3552 defines a Binding Operational Directive as 'a compulsory direction to an agency' for safeguarding federal information systems. The June 2026 order asked CISA for directives to protect federal systems from AI-enabled attacks. The proposed AI Kill Switch Act would give DHS, acting through CISA, real power to order labs to act.

items.p: Match each standing federal tool to what it actually does.
pairs: CFIUS
Reviews foreign investments in and acquisitions of US businesses
FTC Act Section 5
Bars unfair or deceptive practices in commerce
Section 232 (Trade Expansion Act)
Lets the President adjust imports that threaten national security
FASCSA (Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act)
Lets agencies exclude vendors that pose supply-chain risks
items.x: None of these is a power to halt a domestic lab. CFIUS (the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States) reaches a lab only through a foreign deal, and Section 5 is a consumer-protection tool. FASCSA can exclude a vendor from federal purchasing but can't order it to stop. A January 2026 Section 232 proclamation put a 25% duty on certain imported advanced chips.

items.p: Congress has passed no frontier AI law. Name two existing tools the executive branch used or threatened against AI labs in 2026.
items.answer: Examples: an export-control directive restricting access to two Anthropic models (June); a threat to invoke the Defense Production Act against Anthropic (February); supply-chain-risk designations excluding Anthropic from defense purchasing (March); a directive for agencies to stop using Anthropic's technology (February); export controls floated as a way to enforce incident reporting (October).
keys: export-control directive (Commerce, June 2026)
Defense Production Act threat (February 2026)
supply-chain-risk designations or exclusion from purchasing
presidential directive to stop federal use
export controls floated to enforce incident reporting
items.x: Most relied on laws not written with AI labs in mind, and the presidential directive cited no law at all, so the legal fights were over how far existing laws reach. In October 2026 an official also floated export controls as a way to enforce a new White House incident-reporting system that had no set definitions or penalties yet.

choice.p: Which of these did the US executive branch actually use or threaten against an AI lab in 2026?
o: A threat to invoke the Defense Production Act
An IEEPA order blocking a US lab's transactions with American customers
A CISA Binding Operational Directive ordering a lab to shut a model down
A Communications Act takeover of a lab's data center
ow: No IEEPA order was used against a lab; IEEPA needs a threat from abroad and foreign interests.
These directives bind only federal agencies' own systems.
No such takeover was reported; the hard moves in 2026 were export controls and procurement.

units.title: The courts as a check
units.desc: How judges limit emergency action: reading statutes by their text, no deference to agencies, narrower injunctions, free speech and payment for property taken.

items.p: Biden v. Nebraska (2023) tested a law letting the Education Secretary 'waive or modify' loan rules in connection with a national emergency. What did the Court decide?
o: The power to 'modify' allows only modest changes, so it couldn't cancel about $430 billion in loans
The emergency power allowed the cancellation, since emergency laws are read broadly by courts
The case was dismissed because the COVID emergency had ended before the Court could rule
The cancellation stood because Congress failed to pass a resolution blocking it within 30 days
ow: The Court read 'modify' narrowly, emergency or not.
The Court decided the merits and struck down the cancellation plan.
The law had no such resolution procedure.
keys: the emergency power didn't allow mass loan cancellation
'modify' allows modest adjustments, not transformation
an emergency trigger doesn't stretch a statute's words
items.x: The Court said the power to modify allows 'modest adjustments and additions to existing provisions,' not transforming them. It's an example of the Court applying major-questions reasoning to a power triggered by an emergency, the same move three justices made explicit in the 2026 tariff case.

items.p: After Loper Bright v. Raimondo (2024), suppose an agency reads an ambiguous old statute as letting it regulate AI labs. What changed about how courts review that reading?
o: Courts decide the statute's best meaning themselves, without deferring to the agency's reading
Courts still defer to the agency's reading of an ambiguous statute if the reading is reasonable
Courts can no longer review an agency's reading of a statute once it has gone through public comment
Agencies must now get Congress's approval before adopting a new reading of an older statute
ow: That was Chevron deference, which Loper Bright overruled.
Review continues; what ended was deference.
No such approval requirement exists.
keys: Chevron overruled
courts no longer defer to agency readings of ambiguous statutes
items.x: The Court said courts 'need not and under the APA may not defer to an agency interpretation of the law simply because a statute is ambiguous.' Its reach in an AI emergency may be limited, though: it interprets the Administrative Procedure Act, the President isn't an agency under that Act, and export-control actions are exempt from its review provisions.

items.p: After Trump v. CASA (2025), suppose one AI lab sues and wins against a federal order restricting all frontier models. Why might the win not stop the order for every lab?
items.answer: CASA held that universal injunctions likely exceed federal courts' authority, so relief generally covers the lab that sued (and class members, if a class is certified), not every lab the order covers. CASA left open whether courts can vacate an agency action for everyone under the Administrative Procedure Act.
keys: universal injunctions likely exceed courts' authority
relief generally covers the plaintiff or a certified class
vacating agency action under the APA was left open
items.x: CASA said relief should be what is 'necessary to provide complete relief to each plaintiff with standing to sue.' For AI, each covered company might need its own suit or a class action. CASA left open whether courts can vacate an agency action for everyone under the Administrative Procedure Act, which could matter for an agency order.

choice.p: After Trump v. CASA (2025), one AI lab sues and wins an injunction against a federal order restricting frontier models. Who does the injunction generally protect?
o: The lab that sued, plus class members if a class is certified, but not every lab the order covers
Every company the order covers, anywhere in the country, from the moment the judge signs the injunction
Only the lab's customers, since the injunction protects users rather than companies
No one, until the Supreme Court reviews and affirms the lower court's ruling
ow: The Court held universal injunctions likely exceed federal courts' authority.
Relief goes to the plaintiff with standing to sue.
An injunction takes effect when issued unless a court stays it.

items.p: A halt order would stop a lab from publishing a model's weights. Lawyers flag the First Amendment. How settled is the law here?
o: Unsettled: some rulings treat code as speech, but whether model weights count is an open question
Settled: courts have held that model weights are commercial products without speech protection
Settled: the Supreme Court held in 1999 that computer source code is protected as speech
Unsettled, since free speech protections are partly suspended during a declared national emergency
ow: No court has held this.
The 1999 ruling, Bernstein v. DOJ, came from a Ninth Circuit panel, and that opinion was withdrawn for rehearing; the Supreme Court never ruled.
The First Amendment applies in emergencies; a court blocked the 2020 WeChat ban partly on First Amendment grounds.
keys: untested for model weights
code-as-speech precedent exists but isn't settled (Bernstein withdrawn)
prior restraint doctrine could apply
items.x: In Bernstein v. DOJ (1999), a divided Ninth Circuit panel treated encryption source code as protected expression, but the court withdrew that opinion to rehear the case. The Sixth Circuit in Junger v. Daley (2000) also held source code protected, but neither case addressed model weights. Courts strongly disfavor prior restraints on speech.

items.p: If the government took control of an AI lab's data center in a crisis, what would the Constitution require it to do for the owner?
o: Pay just compensation, as for coal mines seized in World War II
No payment is owed if the President declared a national emergency beforehand
Return the property within 30 days unless Congress votes to extend the takeover
Get a court warrant first; with one, no payment is owed for using the property
ow: Declaring an emergency doesn't suspend the Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause.
No such 30-day rule exists.
The duty is to pay for what is taken; a warrant doesn't replace compensation.
keys: just compensation
Fifth Amendment Takings Clause
United States v. Pewee Coal (1951)
items.x: After a 1943 order seized struck coal mines, Justice Black's opinion for four justices in United States v. Pewee Coal (1951) said: 'Having taken Pewee's property, the United States became liable under the Constitution to pay just compensation.' Justice Reed concurred, making a 5 to 4 judgment. Section 706 of the Communications Act also builds in just compensation for facilities it takes over.

units.title: Congress as a check
units.desc: Congress can end emergencies, let powers expire, cut off money and write narrower laws, but most of these depend on a majority willing to act.

items.p: Can Congress use the Congressional Review Act to overturn a presidential executive order on AI?
o: No: the Act covers rules issued by agencies, and the President isn't an agency
Yes: simple majorities can overturn an executive action within 60 days of its issue
Yes, but just for orders the President issues under a declared national emergency
No: overturning an executive order is a power reserved to the federal courts
ow: The Act applies to agency rules, not presidential directives.
The Act doesn't single out emergency orders.
Congress can override an order by passing an ordinary law (subject to veto), and courts can strike orders down.
keys: the Act covers agency rules
the President is not an agency
it doesn't apply to executive orders
items.x: CRS: 'No, the CRA does not apply to actions of the President such as executive orders and other types of presidential directives.' Congress can still pass an ordinary bill to override an order, but the President can veto it.

items.p: A 2026 House bill, the ARTICLE ONE Act, would make national emergencies lapse after 30 days unless Congress passes a joint resolution approving them. Why would that be a stronger check than current law?
o: If Congress does nothing, the emergency ends, so the President has no veto to use against Congress
It would let Congress end emergencies by concurrent resolution, which the President can't veto
It would move the decision to the courts, which can end emergencies faster than Congress
It would require the President to name the statutes he will use, which current law doesn't require
ow: The bill keeps joint resolutions; its change is to require approval in place of termination.
Courts get no role under the bill; Congress's inaction ends the emergency.
Current law already requires this; the National Emergencies Act bars using powers until the President names them.
keys: flips the burden from ending to approving
if Congress does nothing, the emergency ends
no veto-proof majority needed, unlike today
items.x: Today ending an emergency over the President's objection takes two-thirds of each chamber. Reps. Chip Roy and Steve Cohen introduced the bill (H.R. 10132) in August 2026; it exempts emergencies that use only IEEPA, and it had no action beyond committee referral as of October 2026.

items.p: The National Emergencies Act promises fast-track votes on resolutions to end emergencies. How did the House avoid one on the 2025 tariff emergency?
o: It adopted a rule saying days wouldn't count as calendar days for the Act's deadlines
The Speaker ruled the resolution out of order because it concerned trade policy, not national security
It sent the resolution to a committee that never reported it, which the Act explicitly allows
The President withdrew the emergency just before the vote, then declared it again
ow: The House used a special rule, H.Res. 211, to stop the clock, not a ruling from the chair.
The Act requires committees to report within 15 calendar days; the House stopped the days from counting.
The emergency was not withdrawn.
keys: a House rule (H.Res. 211) stopped the Act's calendar-day clock
so the fast-track deadlines never ran
items.x: The Act requires committee action within 15 calendar days and a floor vote within 3. H.Res. 211 declared that days would not count for resolutions on the emergencies declared February 1, 2025. The Senate passed a resolution ending the Canada tariff emergency 51 to 48 in April 2025, but the House held it at the desk. In February 2026 a bid to extend the freeze failed, and the House passed its own resolution to end that emergency, 219 to 211. Checks depend on a majority wanting to use them.

items.p: Besides passing a resolution to end an emergency, name two ways Congress can limit the executive's emergency powers over AI.
items.answer: Examples: let a power expire at its sunset or attach conditions when renewing it (the DPA's core powers expire December 11, 2026); appropriations riders barring spending on an action; reporting requirements; a statute that narrows or replaces an authority; making a new AI statute the only legal route for halts; oversight hearings.
keys: sunsets and conditions at renewal
appropriations riders
reporting requirements
new statutes that narrow or replace an authority
oversight hearings
items.x: Sunsets work differently from termination votes: if Congress does nothing, the power ends, and there's nothing for the President to veto. The FRONTIER Act would make its emergency section 'the exclusive means' for any official, including the President, to halt a frontier model on catastrophic-risk grounds.

choice.p: Which of these is a way Congress can limit emergency powers without needing to override a veto?
o: Let a power expire at its sunset date instead of renewing it
Pass a concurrent resolution ending the emergency
Use the Congressional Review Act against the President's emergency order
Have the Senate alone vote to cancel the emergency
ow: Concurrent resolutions haven't been able to end emergencies since 1985.
The Congressional Review Act doesn't cover presidential orders.
Both chambers must act, and the President can veto.

items.p: Put these events in order, tracing how Congress's power to end national emergencies developed.
items: Congress passes the National Emergencies Act, letting it end emergencies without the President
The Supreme Court strikes down legislative vetoes in INS v. Chadha
Congress amends the Act so ending an emergency takes a joint resolution the President can veto
Both chambers pass a resolution ending a national emergency for the first time, and the veto holds
items.x: 1976, 1983, 1985, 2019. The 1976 Act built a strong check for Congress, Chadha struck that kind of check down, and the 1985 fix made ending an emergency vetoable, which is why the 2019 effort failed.

units.title: Designing an AI halt power
units.desc: The 2026 bills and proposals for AI-specific shutdown powers: who decides, when they can act, and the safeguards meant to keep the power from being abused.

items.p: Under the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925, introduced July 2026), who could order a frontier AI model suspended, and on what finding?
o: The Commerce Secretary, on finding the model poses an imminent catastrophic risk
The Homeland Security Secretary, after a covered incident has already occurred
The President, after declaring a national emergency over the model
An independent AI safety board, by majority vote after holding a public hearing on the model
ow: That describes the Lieu-Moran AI Kill Switch Act, which works through DHS and CISA.
The bill gives the power to Commerce and makes it the only route, including for the President.
The bill creates no independent board for this.
keys: the Secretary of Commerce
a finding of imminent catastrophic risk
items.x: 'Imminent catastrophic risk' means a present or impending, foreseeable and material risk that the model materially contributes to death or serious injury of more than 50 people, or more than $1 billion in damage, in one incident involving weapons help, harmful conduct without human oversight, or evading control. Provisional orders lapse within 45 days and final orders after 90 unless renewed on a new finding. As of October 2026 the bill had no markup.

items.p: The FRONTIER Act and the AI Kill Switch Act would both let the government stop a model. What's the key difference in when each lets it act?
o: FRONTIER can act on an imminent risk before harm; the Kill Switch Act acts after an incident
FRONTIER waits until deaths have occurred; the Kill Switch Act can act on a risk before harm
Both need Congress to approve each specific order by joint resolution within a set number of days
FRONTIER covers models still in training; the Kill Switch Act covers models already released
ow: Reversed: FRONTIER's trigger is 'a present or impending catastrophic risk,' and the Kill Switch Act acts after a covered incident.
Neither bill requires Congress to approve individual orders.
FRONTIER covers development, deployment and internal use.
keys: FRONTIER: a present or impending catastrophic risk, before harm
Kill Switch Act: after a covered incident has occurred
items.x: The Kill Switch Act's covered incidents include sabotaging a lawful shutdown instruction, concealment from monitoring, a loss-of-control scenario, or unintended conduct causing at least 10 deaths or $100 million in damage. The tradeoff: acting before harm can prevent it but rests on a prediction; acting after an incident is easier to justify but later.

items.p: A halt power can let officials act on an imminent risk, before any harm, or only after an incident has happened. What's the main tradeoff between those two designs?
items.answer: Acting on imminent risk can stop harm before it happens, but it rests on a prediction that officials could get wrong or misuse. Acting only after an incident is easier to justify and check, but some damage has already been done.
keys: acting before harm can prevent it
but relies on predictions that can be wrong or misused
acting after an incident is easier to justify but comes later
items.x: The FRONTIER Act takes the first approach ('a present or impending catastrophic risk'); the Lieu-Moran AI Kill Switch Act takes the second (after a 'covered incident'). The FRONTIER Act pairs its trigger with written findings, hearings, lapse dates and court review.

choice.p: What's the main tradeoff between letting a halt power act on imminent risk and letting it act only after an incident?
o: Acting early can prevent harm but rests on predictions that can be wrong or misused
Acting early is cheaper, but courts can't review orders made before harm occurs
Acting after an incident is faster, since the facts are already known to everyone
Acting after an incident needs Congress's approval, so it is more accountable
ow: Orders made before harm can be reviewed; the FRONTIER Act provides hearings and court review.
Waiting for an incident means acting later, not faster.
Neither 2026 bill requires Congress to approve individual orders.

items.p: Match each 2026 AI bill to what it would do about shutting down AI systems.
pairs: FRONTIER Act
Commerce may suspend a model on finding imminent catastrophic risk
AI Kill Switch Act
DHS may order a shutdown or other proportionate action after a covered incident
AI Emergency Button Act
Requires a human shutdown capability; gives the government no order power
Stop Rogue AI Act
NIST security standards for AI agents used by agencies and contractors
items.x: Only the first two would let the government order anything. Names can mislead: the Stop Rogue AI Act is about inventorying, identifying and monitoring agents, and the Emergency Button Act only makes sure an off switch exists. None had passed as of October 2026, and all die when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027.

items.p: The FRONTIER Act would make its emergency-order process 'the exclusive means' for any official to halt a frontier model on catastrophic-risk grounds. If it were law, could Commerce repeat a June 2026-style export-control restriction for that purpose?
o: No: it would have to use the Act's process, with written findings, lapse dates and court review
Yes: export controls rest on a separate law, ECRA, and the bill leaves that law untouched
Yes, as long as the President personally signed off on the restriction first
No, because the bill repeals the Export Control Reform Act and with it Commerce's licensing powers
ow: Export controls stay for other purposes, but halts on catastrophic-risk grounds would have to use the Act's process.
Exclusivity covers every official, including the President.
The bill doesn't repeal export-control law; it channels catastrophic-risk halts into one process.
keys: no: catastrophic-risk halts must go through the Act's process
exclusivity reaches other statutes, including export controls, for that purpose
the process includes findings, lapse dates and review
items.x: It could bear on episodes like the June 2026 export directive, depending on the grounds the government gives. Afterward, Lawfare's Alan Rozenshtein (who works at Anthropic) argued that if Washington treats frontier models as switchable assets, Congress should set the standards and process; ARI's Brad Carson said such decisions need insulation from impulse and political favoritism.

items.p: Match each safeguard proposed for AI halt powers to the abuse it is meant to prevent.
pairs: Order lapses after 72 hours unless a court extends it
A halt that outlasts the emergency with no outside review
Written findings stating the factual basis
Arbitrary or unexplained decisions
Copies of every order sent to Congress within days
Halts ordered out of public and legislative view
One statute as the only legal route for halts
Officials improvising with laws written for other purposes
items.x: The 72-hour lapse comes from Americans for Responsible Innovation's August 2026 blueprint; written findings, copies to Congress within 3 days, and exclusivity are in the FRONTIER Act. ARI also proposes limiting the power to named senior officials and ending its whole regime after nine years unless renewed.
